BOOK ENTRY
The prophet that teacheth lies — Isaiah's own decode, with head and tail already defined by the covenant: obedience makes Israel “the head, and not the tail,” and the curse inverts it. The dragon fells a third of the stars with its tail — the led destroyed by the misleading — and the trumpet armies' serpent-tails “had heads”: the liar enthroned. Moses is told to seize the serpent exactly there.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 9:15-16; Deut 28:13, 44; Rev 12:4; 9:19; Ex 4:4) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 9:15 — The ancient and honourable, he is the head; and the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail.
Isaiah 9:16 — For the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are destroyed.
Deuteronomy 28:13 — And the LORD shall make thee the head, and not the tail; and thou shalt be above only, and thou shalt not be beneath; if that thou hearken unto the commandments of the LORD thy God, which I command thee this day, to observe and to do them:
Deuteronomy 28:44 — He shall lend to thee, and thou shalt not lend to him: he shall be the head, and thou shalt be the tail.
Revelation 12:4 — And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth: and the dragon stood before the woman which was ready to be delivered, for to devour her child as soon as it was born.
Revelation 9:19 — For their power is in their mouth, and in their tails: for their tails were like unto serpents, and had heads, and with them they do hurt.
Exodus 4:4 — And the LORD said unto Moses, Put forth thine hand, and take it by the tail. And he put forth his hand, and caught it, and it became a rod in his hand:

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the Scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” that the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, Scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very Scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

PRIOR FINDINGS ACCEPTED BY THIS PROVIDER AND MODEL IN FROZEN RUNS
No prior findings were supplied.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/35-the-fall-of-babylon.adoc

When the victors over the beast stand on the sea of glass at the end of the story, listen to what they sing:

And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast… And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb…

Why the song of Moses — the song Israel sang on the far shore of the Red Sea (Exodus 15:1)?
Because the deliverance they have just come through is the same deliverance.
The Exodus is not only history; it is the similitude of the Fall of Babylon — scene for scene, as Jonah was scene for scene the Passion.
Lay the two side by side.

The first plague turned the waters of Egypt to blood; the vials turn the sea and rivers to blood, and this time the interpretation is spoken aloud (Revelation 16:6). [Footnote: The vial verses are quoted and worked in full in the Sea & Waters chapter.]
The waters are “peoples, and multitudes, and nations” (Revelation 17:15) — the equation the sign-of-Jonah chapter first put to work — so waters turned to blood are death upon the peoples, their own shed blood given back to them; the Sea study in Part Six works the full equation.

The hands that wield the plagues are the same office.
Look at the commission of the two witnesses:

These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will.

These are Moses and Aaron’s credentials, reissued at the end of the age.
Pharaoh had his court magicians; Babylon has her sorceries (Revelation 18:23).
The contest is the same contest, at full scale.

The contest opened, both times, with one enacted sign — a similitude acted out before a word was argued.
“What is that in thine hand? And he said, A rod. And he said, Cast it on the ground. And he cast it on the ground, and it became a serpent” (Exodus 4:2-3).
The rod is no neutral stick: the Hebrew matteh means staff and tribe in one word — when the princes bring twelve rods, they are the twelve tribes by the language itself (Numbers 17:2) — and Aaron's rod is the rod “for the house of Levi” (Numbers 17:8): the priesthood in his hand.
Cast to the earth, the priesthood-rod turns serpent — and before Pharaoh the word sharpens: there it becomes a tannin, a dragon, the devouring kingdom — and “Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods” (Exodus 7:12).
The priesthood, gone serpentine, does not merely join the dragons of the nations; it swallows them and rides what remains.
John saw where that ends:

And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS… The seven heads are seven mountains, on which the woman sitteth… And the woman which thou sawest is that great city, which reigneth over the kings of the earth.

Only a covenant partner can wear the harlot's title.
A harlot is not an outsider; she is a wife gone traitor — harlotry is covenant defected, and only a covenant people can commit it: “How is the faithful city become an harlot!” (Isaiah 1:21).
And this great city is identified by its crime scene: “the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified” (Revelation 11:8) — Jerusalem.
The woman riding the beast is the covenant order gone serpent — Aaron's rod cast down, astride the seven heads it swallowed — the mother whose daughter-harlots learned the trade in her house.
The name on her forehead is not her own.
Babylon the Great names the beast she rides, and she wears it where the seal goes: the saints carry the Father's name in their foreheads (Revelation 14:1); Babylon's own carry “the mark of his name” (Revelation 14:11).
The wife who left her Husband's name is branded with her owner's — the beast's mark in the seal's place.

Jeremiah's oracle fixes the last Babylon at the end in more than one sense.
“Your mother shall be sore confounded… behold, the hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness” (Jeremiah 50:12).
The Hebrew acharith is the last or end — what comes after.
In the immediate judgment, the “glory of kingdoms” is brought last in rank (Isaiah 13:19).
In the prophetic succession, Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon stood at the head of gold — “thou art this head of gold” — while Babylon the Great appears at the latter end, when the stone strikes the image's feet (Daniel 2:34-35, 38, 44-45).
Babylon frames man's image: the original kingdom at its head, the final Babylon at its feet.

The word also carries a direction.
Scripture's compass faces east — qedem is at once “east” and “front” — so west lies behind.
The related after/back/end word-family names the western sea the “hinder sea” (Deuteronomy 11:24; Zechariah 14:8).
Jeremiah need not be made to choose among the layers: Babylon is brought last in rank, appears last in the imperial succession, and sits hindermost — westernmost — among the nations.
The last Babylon sits at the far west of the nations: a bloc of seven mountains that even counts itself as seven, ridden by the city that killed the prophets, its base of power the westernmost nation of them all.

The similitude has a third act, and it was in Moses' hand from the beginning.
“Put forth thine hand, and take it by the tail. And he put forth his hand, and caught it, and it became a rod in his hand” (Exodus 4:4).
Every word is loaded.
The tail is decoded in-text by Isaiah: “the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail” (Isaiah 9:15) — the serpent is seized at its lying-prophet end.
And watch the dragon wield that member:

And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth.

The stars are the saints, and Daniel shows the same fall with the trampling included: the horn “cast down some of the host and of the stars to the ground, and stamped upon them” (Daniel 8:10).
The dragon fells a third of heaven's host not with claws but with its tail — by the prophet that teaches lies — for “the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are destroyed” (Isaiah 9:16).
The trumpet armies carry the same reversal — “their power is in their mouth, and in their tails: for their tails were like unto serpents, and had heads” (Revelation 9:19) — tails grown heads, which is the covenant curse in one clause: “he shall be the head, and thou shalt be the tail” (Deuteronomy 28:44), the inversion of the blessing that made obedient Israel “the head, and not the tail” (Deuteronomy 28:13).
So the command to seize the serpent by the tail is the countermove itself: take the liar's instrument in hand, and it is mastered.
The Hebrew for “caught” is chazaq — the very verb of the whole contest, for “I will harden [chazaq] Pharaoh's heart” (Exodus 4:21): the hand that chazaq-grips the serpent turns it back into the staff of God; the heart that chazaq-hardens itself belongs to the serpent.
One verb, two grips.
Revelation keeps the scene for the end: “he laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent… and bound him” (Revelation 20:2).

The rod that comes back is not bare wood.
Set overnight before the testimony, “the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” (Numbers 17:8) — the dead stick alive, the priesthood proven by resurrection.
The almond is the shaqed, the watcher-tree, first to wake — “I see a rod of an almond tree… for I will watch over my word to perform it” (Jeremiah 1:11-12) — and the lampstand of the sanctuary is carved as this very tree, its bowls “made like unto almonds” (Exodus 25:33): the watcher-tree bears the lamp, and the lamp, Scripture says, is the commandment (Proverbs 6:23).

An almond is a fruit that is itself a seed — and “the seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11).
Root to crown the watcher-tree carries nothing but the word: its blossom the priesthood's proof, its fruit the seed-word, its carved form the commandment's lampstand.
Rod, serpent, rod again — and then blossom: the priesthood cast down and gone dragon is seized at the liar's tail, restored to the Owner's palm, and buds with the resurrection sign.
The similitude that opened the first exodus is the arc of the last one.

The demand carried to Pharaoh — “let my people go, that they may serve me” (Exodus 8:1) — returns as the last call of the book:

And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.

Jeremiah had already given Babylon the same summons:

My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver ye every man his soul from the fierce anger of the LORD.

One voice, three ages: out of Egypt, out of Babylon, out of Babylon the great.
The people of God end every act of the story by walking out of a doomed house — and the plagues fall on those who stay.

The destruction enters from a specific quarter.
“For, lo, I will raise and cause to come up against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the north country” (Jeremiah 50:9); “a people shall come from the north, and a great nation” (Jeremiah 50:41); “the spoilers shall come unto her from the north” (Jeremiah 51:48).
The word itself tells you why the destroyer owns that door.
“North” — tsaphon — is the hidden quarter, the lurker's quarter: the dark one, the direction the ambush comes from. [Footnote: The word study — tsaphan, to hide by covering over, to lurk — is in the Lucifer's Declared Plan chapter.]

The north behaves this way throughout the prophets: “out of the north an evil shall break forth” (Jeremiah 1:14) — and when the evil comes, it comes like a predator from cover, “the lion is come up from his thicket, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way” (Jeremiah 4:7); the spoiler, the robber-word, falls suddenly on the unwatchful (Jeremiah 6:22-26).
Robbers work from the dark — “in the dark they dig through houses… they know not the light” (Job 24:16) — and the north is the sky's own dark, the one quarter the sun never crosses.

The word carries both of its appearances in this book at once: the north country is the hidden quarter where Babylon's spoilers gather, and the sides of the north — the uttermost recesses of that dark — are the address the enemy chose for his own seat (Lucifer’s Declared Plan).
The lurker who worked from the hidden dark is repaid out of it: the spoiler comes upon Babylon from the door she cannot watch.

Now the ending both stories share.
When the pursuer followed Israel into the sea, the song names his end twice: “they sank into the bottom as a stone” (Exodus 15:5); “they sank as lead in the mighty waters” (Exodus 15:10) — “their persecutors thou threwest into the deeps, as a stone into the mighty waters” (Nehemiah 9:11).
Jeremiah turned that ending into a commanded sign: the scroll of Babylon’s judgment bound to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates —

…thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of Euphrates: And thou shalt say, Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her…

Revelation performs the sign at scale:

And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all.

This is a phrase-symbol in its own right — cast into the sea, a ruling power sunk into the sea of peoples, never to surface; the Sea study in Part Six gathers its every use.
The mountain that destroyed all the earth is rolled down and burned (Jeremiah 51:25); the millstone goes under; the music stops (Revelation 18:22).

Jesus put this very sign into His disciples' mouths, twice.
“Whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart… he shall have whatsoever he saith” (Mark 11:23) — and a parallel saying runs on the other kingdom-figure: “ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea” (Luke 17:6).
A mountain is a kingdom and, at this scale, a tree is a nation; what faith commands into the sea is not landscaping — it is Babylon's sentence, spoken by the household of faith.

And Revelation shows the mechanism in order: the incense goes up “with the prayers of all saints” (Revelation 8:3-4), the censer is cast to the earth, and at the second trumpet “as it were a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea” (Revelation 8:8) — Jeremiah's burnt mountain, over the cliff at last.
The prayers ascend; the mountain falls.
Faith that moves mountains was never about landscaping either — it is the saints praying down the destroying mountain, and being heard.

The sentence keeps the going-down separate from the verdict.
Everyone in these stories goes into the waters.
Babylon sinks “and shall not rise.”

Jonah went into the same sea and rose; the Messiah went into the heart of the earth and could not be held by it (Acts 2:24); and every convert enacts the split in baptism, going under into death and coming up in newness of life (Romans 6:4), his sins staying down like Babylon (Micah 7:19). [Footnote: The rising half of the contrast is drawn scene by scene in the Sign of Jonah chapter.]
The waters take everyone; the covenant decides who comes up.

The coming up is the difference between the lawless kingdom and the righteous man in the same flood — and it is why the millstone is also a personal warning: better one “hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6) than to make the little ones stumble.
A man can be Babylon in miniature.

Who is she?
Revelation defines both coordinates in one chapter: the waters where the whore sitteth are the waters already identified — peoples, multitudes, and nations (Revelation 17:15) — and “the woman which thou sawest is that great city, which reigneth over the kings of the earth” (Revelation 17:18).
The title has a history — Nineveh wore it three times (Jonah 1:2; 3:2; 4:11), and the sign-of-Jonah chapter traced where it points.
Babylon swallowed God’s people “like a dragon” (Jeremiah 51:34) — and the dragon, we saw with Jonah, is made to give back what it swallowed.

Revelation does more than describe the great city; it gives her street address, and gives it in the book's own symbolic grammar:

And their dead bodies shall lie in the street of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified.

One city, three names.
Where was the Lord crucified? — there is one answer, and every reader knows it.
And the verse says the other two names are what that city is called spiritually — the very kind of writing the woman carries on her forehead: “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS” (Revelation 17:5) — a mystery-inscription; and in the seal's own grammar, the name on a forehead names the one she belongs to.

Nor did Revelation invent the method.
Isaiah stood in Jerusalem and addressed her rulers to their faces:

Hear the word of the LORD, ye rulers of Sodom; give ear unto the law of our God, ye people of Gomorrah.

Ezekiel makes the kinship formal: “thine elder sister is Samaria… and thy younger sister… is Sodom” (Ezekiel 16:46).
The prophets already called Jerusalem Sodom when she lived like Sodom.

Egypt is the same grammar.
Egypt is “the house of bondage” (Exodus 20:2) — and Paul writes of “Jerusalem which now is,” that she “is in bondage with her children” (Galatians 4:25): the covenant city living as the slave-house is called by the slave-house's name.
Ezekiel had already watched her earn it: Jerusalem the harlot “multiplied her whoredoms” in remembering “the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt” (Ezekiel 23:19).

The last identifying mark is blood.
In the great city “was found the blood of prophets, and of saints” (Revelation 18:24) — and Jesus fixed that address forever: “upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth” (Matthew 23:35); “it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33); “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets” (Matthew 23:37).
Sodom for her sin, Egypt for her bondage — and on her brow her owner's name, Babylon, the beast's mark — and the street where the witnesses lie dead runs through the city that crucified her King.
The unfaithful wife of the marriage chapter and the boasting queen of the widows’ chapter are the same woman, and her own name is not a foreign capital's.

The sea of glass scene now reads whole.
The victors stand where Israel stood — on the far side of the waters that drowned their pursuer — and they sing the same song, doubled: “the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb.”
The first Exodus gave the pattern; the last performs it on every nation at once: plagues on the oppressor, a people called out, the pursuer sunk like a stone, and a shore with singing on it.
“Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise.”
The gospel the book has been reading all along ends exactly where it began at the Red Sea: the kingdom that would not let go, gone under the waters — and the people of God standing on glass, dry-shod, learning the old song by heart.
